title: Monte Carlo tree search
text:
### Monte Carlo method

The Monte Carlo method, which uses random sampling for deterministic problems which are difficult or impossible to solve using other approaches, dates back to the 1940s.[1] In his 1987 PhD thesis, Bruce Abramson combined minimax search with an expected-outcome model based on random game playouts to the end, instead of the usual static evaluation function. Abramson said the expected-outcome model "is shown to be precise, accurate, easily estimable, efficiently calculable, and domain-independent."[2] He experimented in-depth with tic-tac-toe and then with machine-generated evaluation functions for Othello and chess.

Such methods were then explored and successfully applied to heuristic search in the field of automated theorem proving by W. Ertel, J. Schumann and C. Suttner in 1989,[3,4,5] thus improving the exponential search times of uninformed search algorithms such as e.g. breadth-first search, depth-first search or iterative deepening.

In 1992, B. Brügmann employed it for the first time in a Go-playing program.[6] In 2002, Chang et al.[7] proposed the idea of "recursive rolling out and backtracking" with "adaptive" sampling choices in their Adaptive Multi-stage Sampling (AMS) algorithm for the model of Markov decision processes. AMS was the first work to explore the idea of UCB-based exploration and exploitation in constructing sampled/simulated (Monte Carlo) trees and was the main seed for UCT (Upper Confidence Trees).[8]

### Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS)

In 2006, inspired by its predecessors,[9] Rémi Coulom described the application of the Monte Carlo method to game-tree search and coined the name Monte Carlo tree search,[10] L. Kocsis and Cs. Szepesvári developed the UCT (Upper Confidence bounds applied to Trees) algorithm,[11] and S. Gelly et al. implemented UCT in their program MoGo.[12] In 2008, MoGo achieved dan (master) level in 9×9 Go,[13] and the Fuego program began to win against strong amateur players in 9×9 Go.[14]

In January 2012, the Zen program won 3:1 in a Go match on a 19×19 board with an amateur 2 dan player.[15] Google Deepmind developed the program AlphaGo, which in October 2015 became the first Computer Go program to beat a professional human Go player without handicaps on a full-sized 19x19 board.[16,17,18] In March 2016, AlphaGo was awarded an honorary 9-dan (master) level in 19×19 Go for defeating Lee Sedol in a five-game match with a final score of four games to one.[19] AlphaGo represents a significant improvement over previous Go programs as well as a milestone in machine learning as it uses Monte Carlo tree search with artificial neural networks (a deep learning method) for policy (move selection) and value, giving it efficiency far surpassing previous programs.[20]

The MCTS algorithm has also been used in programs that play other board games (for example Hex,[21] Havannah,[22] Game of the Amazons,[23] and Arimaa[24]), real-time video games (for instance Ms. Pac-Man[25,26] and Fable Legends[27]), and nondeterministic games (such as skat,[28] poker,[29] Magic: The Gathering,[30] or Settlers of Catan[31]).
